title: Embedding dimensioning, batching & SLO cost discussion - AcmeAI
summary: Redwood SE and AE reviewed embedding dimensionality tradeoffs, batching strategies, KV-cache interactions for reranking workloads, quantization impacts on recall, and deployment constraints for VPC/on-prem. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot: perf matrix + cost model + security checklist.
topics: KV cache hit rates and prefix caching
VPC/private deployment constraints and PCI-data residency
next_steps: Redwood to share cost-per-embedding bench CSV and perf spreadsheet
AcmeAI to provide sample dataset (5k queries + 50k corpus) for pilot
Schedule infra handshake call for VPC peering and egress limits w/ Laura
action_items: Jordan Patel - run dimension sweep (64/128/256/512) with 1k qps synthetic workload - due 2025-09-12
Maya Torres - send security one-pager and SOC2 artifact links (security-pack.pdf) - due 2025-09-05
Samir Gupta - deliver sample dataset and current rerank baseline (notebooks/metrics) - due 2025-09-09
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Torres: Hi everyone, thanks for jumping on. We planned 60 minutes to go through embeddings sizing, batching, and cost tradeoffs for the rerank flow.
[00:08] Samir Gupta: Hey Maya, yeah thanks. We're trying to get to a predictable cost curve and stay under 50ms tail latency for the top-k rerank stage.
[00:15] Jordan Patel: Great, quick intro - I'm Jordan on the Redwood infra side, I typically run perf benchmarks and kernel selection.
[00:22] Ben Wallace: Ben from product - I care mostly about user-perceived latency and budget for inference.
[00:27] Nina Flores: Nina, data science, I care about recall hit rates and stable rankings when we change dims/quant.
[00:33] Laura Chen: Laura, infra, I'll flag anything network/VPC related.
[00:40] Maya Torres: Cool. Samir, can you remind us of the current pipeline? You mentioned top-k rerank after vector search?
[00:47] Samir Gupta: Right; we do a hybrid: ANN index returns top 200, then we run a BERT-based reranker over those 200. Embeddings currently 768 dims, float32, hosted in our cluster. Cost is high and tail latency sometimes spikes to 120-200ms which is too slow.
[01:05] Jordan Patel: Okay, so two levers: lower embedding dims and move to quantized embeddings / lower precision to cut RAM and network cost; plus batching at the rerank step. But batching increases latency if not micro-batched correctly.
[01:20] Ben Wallace: On business side, if we can shave 30-40% of cost without hurting recall much that's a win.
[01:25] Maya Torres: Jordan, can you walk through how Redwood would profile dims and batching?
[01:30] Jordan Patel: Sure. First, we run a dimension sweep: generate embeddings at 64/128/256/512/768 using the same model family or smaller family if needed. For each dim we measure: embed throughput (embeds/sec), memory per vector, index size, and rerank CPU/GPU latency when scoring batches of N candidates.
[01:47] Jordan Patel: Then we run an end-to-end rerank microbench: simulate 1000 QPS with real sequences, vary batch sizes at rerank (1, 4, 8, 16) and measure p50/p95/p99. We also check KV cache behavior — for rerank we can prefix-cache the first layer activations for the candidate set when we do repeated queries on similar prefixes.
[02:07] Nina Flores: Wait, prefix cache for embeddings? I thought KV cache was more decoder autoreg contexts.
[02:12] Jordan Patel: Yeah, good call — sorry I mean we can cache candidate embeddings and sometimes intermediate scoring values. For the rerank model, if you rerun the same candidate vectors often, an in-memory vector cache or Redis hot-cache reduces repeated embedding recompute or index marshalling cost. Apologies for the slip.
[02:28] Samir Gupta: On our side the heavy part is the BERT reranker scoring 200 candidates; it's doing full cross-attention per candidate, which is expensive. Can we change to a smaller combiner or use approximate rerank?
[02:38] Jordan Patel: You have options: 1) reduce candidate count (e.g., top-100 vs top-200) 2) use a lightweight transformer or MLP reranker for initial pass then a small second-stage BERT for top-10 3) quantize the reranker weights to int8/4bit to reduce GPU mem and increase throughput.
[02:56] Laura Chen: How deterministic is quantization for ranking? We worry about ranking flakiness and legal/regulatory audit trails.
[03:03] Jordan Patel: Quantization can introduce small score shifts. For embeddings themselves, int8 or 4-bit quantization for storage tends to preserve cosine similarity well if you calibrate. For the reranker weights, post-training quantization usually works, but you should run A/B evaluation on held-out queries. We recommend a retrain-aware quantization or per-channel scale factors for stability.
[03:23] Nina Flores: We can't afford recall regression >1% on our core metric. How do we measure that across dims?
[03:28] Jordan Patel: We'll run a recall@k sweep: generate vectors at each dim, reindex, run your Dev queries, compute recall@10/20/100 and NDCG, then estimate cost delta. We'll produce a table showing cost per million queries and recall delta.
[03:39] Ben Wallace: Also curious about the batch sizing tradeoff for user SLOs. We have a 50ms client SLO. If we batch 16 candidates for rerank we might amortize overhead but increase per-request latency.
[03:50] Jordan Patel: Right. For pipelined architecture, one pattern is asynchronous micro-batching: collect requests for a short window (e.g., 5-10ms) and send a batch to the GPU. That keeps tail latency bounded but still uses larger batch sizes for throughput. We can simulate with your latency target and QPS distribution.
[04:07] Samir Gupta: What about KV cache and prefix caching you mentioned earlier? For us many queries are similar across sessions.
[04:12] Jordan Patel: For rerank, candidate embeddings are often reused; keep a hot vector cache on RAM or small GPU memory for top-k candidates, or use a read-through cache in front of the model. Cache hit rate assumptions are important - 5-10% hit rate doesn't move the needle but 40% does. We'll model several hit-rate scenarios.
[04:27] Maya Torres: Let's talk numbers — do you have a sample cost model?
[04:30] Jordan Patel: Yes, we'll share a CSV with per-embed storage, per-embed compute cost, and per-1000 queries cost including network egress. For example, 768-d float32 vectors cost ~3x storage vs 256-d int8. Using quantized 256-d embeddings plus a top-100 candidate set can reduce storage+transfer cost by ~60% in our examples, with <1.5% recall hit in many datasets, but your mileage varies.
[04:55] Laura Chen: Any network egress implications for VPC/private deployment? We must keep data in-region and minimize cross-AZ egress.
[05:02] Jordan Patel: With Redwood Private, you can host the inference plane in your VPC; peering or private link removes public egress. For Hosted, we have region pinning but there is still managed egress. We'll include a network diagram and the peering checklist.
[05:16] Nina Flores: Regarding model selection — are we constrained to one model or can we route cheaper batches to smaller models?
[05:22] Maya Torres: You can do model routing: cheap model for recall candidates, larger for final top-10, and automatic fallback between variants if latency/throughput constraints require. That reduces average cost.
[05:31] Samir Gupta: For pilot, we want to test: 256 vs 512 dims, int8 quantized storage, top-100 vs top-200, and batch sizes 1/4/8 with async micro-batching.
[05:42] Jordan Patel: Sounds good. We'll run an API-level benchmark and a backend rerank bench. For the rerank bench we'll do p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, and token/score throughput.
[05:53] Ben Wallace: How will we validate ranking quality is acceptable?
[05:56] Jordan Patel: We'll compute A/B NDCG and recall on your baseline held-out set. Also run online canary if you want production validation — Redwood supports canary rollouts per-customer.
[06:07] Laura Chen: Security question: we need SAML SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration — plus SOC2 artifacts.
[06:15] Maya Torres: We'll send the SOC2 report and our security one-pager. For Private customers, KMS/HSM integration is available and audit logs can be retained in your logging stack. (see security-pack.pdf)
[06:28] Samir Gupta: Good. Also, what's the expected engineering lift for Private vs Hosted?
[06:33] Maya Torres: Hosted is near-zero infra lift, you call our API. Private requires some infra work: VPC peering or private link, config of load balancers, assigning GPU pools, and possibly an on-prem package if air-gapped. We'll provide a runbook.
[06:47] Nina Flores: On quantization again, do you recommend quantizing embeddings on ingest only or dynamically in serving?
[06:53] Jordan Patel: Prefer quantize-on-write: store quantized embeddings in your index and serve them. That keeps compute lower at query time. For experiments you can keep raw floats and serve quantized copies for inference.
[07:04] Samir Gupta: Let's talk about expected latency numbers — what p95 can we get for a rerank of 100 candidates on a single GPU with int8 weights?
[07:12] Jordan Patel: Rough ballpark: a well-optimized int8 reranker on a modern A100-equivalent can score 100 candidates in ~20-30ms p50, p95 maybe 40-60ms depending on sequence length and batch packing. If you need <50ms p95, combine async micro-batching, smaller model, and pruning to top-50 before heavy rerank.
[07:33] Ben Wallace: That aligns with our goal. But what's the trade for using CPU-only for rerank to save GPU costs?
[07:39] Jordan Patel: CPU-only is much cheaper per hour but latency is higher. For small models and well-optimized kernels, you can do tens of ms p50 but p95 may blow out. GPUs give both throughput and consistent tail. We'll quantify in the benchmark.
[07:52] Maya Torres: We'll share a recommended config matrix: three rows (quality-first, cost-balanced, latency-first) with dims, quant, candidate counts, and estimated cost/QPS.
[08:03] Samir Gupta: Can Redwood help with index format? We're using FAISS on SSDs but considering HNSW in-memory for Hot set.
[08:11] Jordan Patel: Index choice matters. FAISS IVF+PQ is cost-efficient on SSD, HNSW in-memory gives lower lat but higher RAM. For hot items, a hybrid approach works: HNSW for top-100k, IVF for rest. We'll include recommendations.
[08:26] Nina Flores: In earlier trials we saw place-to-place variance: changing vector dim from 512 to 256 sometimes changed topk by >2% which impacted revenue. How do we guard?
[08:36] Jordan Patel: Run similarity-preserving projections (PCA or product quantization tuned) and validate on your metric set. Also can use ensemble scoring — combine 256 and 512 scores for stability during rollout.
[08:48] Laura Chen: On the Private deployment, are there GPU sku constraints? We prefer NVIDIA T4 in our private DC.
[08:54] Jordan Patel: T4 is good for inference, especially with int8. For heavy rerank, V100/A100 class is preferable but T4 in clust scale is cost-effective. We'll map expected throughput per GPU type.
[09:07] Ben Wallace: What's the expected timeline for the pilot?
[09:10] Maya Torres: We suggest 2 weeks for bench runs and cost modeling, then a 4-week pilot for an online canary if metrics are good. So total 6 weeks to pilot completion.
[09:20] Samir Gupta: Fine. Please make sure the pilot doesn't require us to migrate all data. We'll provide a 50k subset.
[09:25] Jordan Patel: That's perfect. We'll run everything on the subset.
[09:28] Maya Torres: Any other blockers?
[09:30] Laura Chen: One: egress and compliance — we need a diagram. Two: network throughput for bulk embedding loads.
[09:36] Maya Torres: We'll include the peering diagram and guidance on chunking bulk loads to avoid throttles.
[09:42] Nina Flores: Also want to test vector dims impact on rerank fairness for minority user cohorts; can we instrument that?
[09:48] Jordan Patel: Yes, add cohort labels to your eval set and we'll stratify the analysis.
[09:52] Ben Wallace: Last item: pricing transparency. We want a per-embed and per-1000-query breakdown.
[09:58] Maya Torres: We'll send a cost spreadsheet (benchmarks/embedding-costs.csv) with assumptions so you can tweak.
[10:05] Samir Gupta: Great. Recap the concrete next steps?
[10:08] Maya Torres: Redwood: run dimension sweep + batching bench, produce CSV and perf report; send security artifacts and runbook. AcmeAI: supply sample dataset and baseline. Joint: schedule VPC peering handshake.
[10:20] Ben Wallace: Sounds good.
[10:22] Maya Torres: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff.
[10:27] Samir Gupta: Thanks.
[10:28] [call ends]
